source.title: Neural Scaling Laws for Jet Generation
source.authors: O. Amram; D. Faroughy; Tjarko Gerdes; Anna Hallin; Gregor Kasieczka; M. Krämer; H. Reyes-González; David Shih

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some equations and figure labels have minor text-extraction formatting artifacts, but the results are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling in jet generation and finds strong parameter-count scaling but substantially weaker dataset-size scaling and poorly resolved compute-optimal model sizes, qualifying how broadly the scaling-law pattern applies.
record.gate_note: The study reports scaling fits for validation loss and sliced Wasserstein distance (SWD), plus an SWD–loss association. The SWD findings concern physical observables, not downstream-task performance as specified in V6. The study cites results from other work, but those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study applies Kaplan-style N and D scaling and a Chinchilla-style isoFLOP analysis to a new setting: an autoregressive transformer trained on tokenized real collider jets. It reports its own loss fits, so it bears on V5 (other modalities), V3 (compute-optimal allocation) and V7 (fit sensitivity). It does not test V1 as stated, because the system is not a language model.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find a clear power law with model size but much weaker, less conclusive scaling with dataset size and compute. They attribute this to a small learnable window and rapid saturation in jet next-token prediction. They also conclude that NTP loss is a good proxy for physics performance (SWD).
record.recipe_differences: The study says its setup is intentionally close in spirit to language-model scaling studies and uses next-token cross-entropy and an isoFLOP analysis. It applies these methods to an autoregressive jet model trained on tokenized collider data, rather than a language model, and includes SWD generation-quality metrics.
record.method_sensitivity: The dataset-size power-law fit is dominated by the D = 6.4×10^6 point; removing it shrinks the fitted dynamic range by a factor of 9. Compute-optimal model size is poorly resolved because the isoFLOP curves are flat and usually lack a clear left flank. Dataset-size runs at the three largest sizes are single-seed.

fits_no_version.finding: Joint SWD on five jet observables follows approximate power laws in N (β=0.506) and D (β=0.914), and is monotonically related to validation NTP loss (Spearman 1.00).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In jet generation, gains in next-token loss with scale translate monotonically into better generated-observable distributions.

record.problems: Dataset-size scaling has comparatively large uncertainty, single-seed results at the three largest dataset sizes, and a fit dominated by the smallest dataset-size point. Compute-optimal fits use five budgets and are explicitly described as poorly resolved because isoFLOP curves are flat and often lack a clear left flank. The text does not report an out-of-sample extrapolation test.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results bearing on the listed claim versions were left out.

untested.parts: No language models are trained; only a jet-generation model is studied.
No test of whether small-run fits predict much larger runs.
Several shape dimensions are varied together with size; there is no comparison of shapes at fixed parameter count.
SWD on jet observables is a generation-quality metric, not downstream-task performance.
The token-count optimum D*(C) is not fitted, and there is no comparison of N versus D growth rates in language models.
Image and video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested.
Parameter-counting conventions, schedules and fitting methods are not systematically varied.

missing.what: Learnable-window diagnostics: the loss change across N covers only 1.6% of W, across D 11.9%, and across D≥3.5e7 only 1.3%, versus 15% for Chinchilla. Even Pico captures 98.4% of W. This bears on how strongly the power law holds in this domain.
Seed-to-seed variability spans almost the entire loss range for D≥3.5e7.
L∞ in the D fit was clamped to min L(D) because the free fit placed L∞ above the largest-D loss; this is a fitting choice. The compute fit uses Nincl rather than non-embedding N.
missing.locator: Sec. II D 2; Sec. II D 3

missing.what: N*(C) fitted from SWD rather than loss gives the same exponent, a=0.92.

record.verdict_notes: V1 links were removed from R1–R3 because V1 names language models; these results are evidence for V5 instead. The tranche was changed from T5 to T3: this is a new-setting test, and it qualifies V5 rather than arguing that a version is wrong. The study is not one of the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests parameter, dataset-size, and compute scaling in one jet-generation setup, but does not establish the claim across language models or other setups.
It fits scaling curves but does not test whether fits from small runs predict the losses of substantially larger runs.
The study fits optimal model size versus compute, but holds dataset size fixed and does not test how the loss-minimizing token count grows with compute or compare parameter and token growth rates.
Model size is varied by changing several architecture dimensions together; the study does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count.
The study tests jet generation on collider data only; it does not test image or video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
SWD measures generated-jet observable distributions, not downstream-task performance.

The study reports sensitivity to one dataset-size fit choice and uncertainty in the compute-optimal fit, but does not systematically vary parameter-counting conventions, training schedules, datasets, or fitting methods.

rows.subject: OmniJet-α
rows.size_stated: Nine sizes, from Pico (N = 2.5×10^4) to XXL (N = 8.5×10^7) non-embedding parameters; 3.5 orders of magnitude.
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size with full dataset and a 400,000-gradient-update training budget; fit validation NTP loss against non-embedding parameter count.
rows.measure: Validation next-token-prediction cross-entropy loss versus non-embedding parameter count
rows.note: The authors describe a clear power law over more than three orders of magnitude in parameter count.
rows.check: V1 names language models; this is a jet-constituent model, so the row bears on V5, not V1. The fit spans 3.5 orders of magnitude in N, but the authors note it covers only 1.6% of the learnable window.

rows.subject: OmniJet-α
rows.operation_detail: Varied unique training-token dataset size and fit minimum validation NTP loss.

conditions.value: Eight sizes spanning three orders of magnitude, from 6.4×10^6 to 8.1×10^9 unique tokens
Three seeds for D ≤ 3.5×10^8; the three largest D were single-seed runs

rows.measure: Minimum validation NTP loss versus unique training-token count D
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals: A_D [3.4×10^3, 9.0×10^4], β_D [0.58, 0.79], L∞ [7.170, 7.195] nats. Single-seed runs have no per-point seed-variance estimate.
rows.note: The authors say the data are compatible with a power law but the dynamic range is small, uncertainty is comparatively large, and the fit is dominated by D = 6.4×10^6; most remaining points are near saturation.
rows.check: Remove V1, since this is not a language model. L∞ was clamped to min L(D), a fitting choice. The fit is dominated by D=6.4e6, and the three largest D are single-seed.

rows.subject: OmniJet-α
rows.size_stated: Sub-Pico through XXL across the tested runs
rows.operation_detail: Compared validation NTP loss across model sizes at five fixed compute budgets using isoFLOP runs.

conditions.value: Five budgets spanning one order of magnitude in FLOPs

rows.measure: Best validation NTP loss across model sizes at fixed compute budgets
rows.value: The isoFLOP curves are unusually flat; even small models are close to the apparent asymptotic limit, and the expected left flank of the U-shape is largely absent.
rows.note: The text describes weakly resolved compute-scaling behavior rather than reporting a fitted validation-loss power law in compute.
rows.check: Remove V1. The isoFLOP curves are flat and lack a left flank. No numeric L*(C) fit is reported in the text, although Eq. 5 is defined.

rows.subject: OmniJet-α
rows.size_stated: Sub-Pico through XXL across the tested runs
rows.operation_detail: Estimated the optimal model size for each compute budget by parabolic interpolation of isoFLOP curves, then fit optimal size against compute.

conditions.value: Parabolic interpolation, with 2,000 bootstrap resamples for uncertainty

rows.measure: Optimal parameter count N*(C) versus compute
rows.locator: Sec. II D 3; Sec. III C; Eq. (12); Figs. 6–7
rows.note: Although the fitted exponent is reported, the authors caution that the optimum is not well resolved because the parabolas are flat and usually lack a clear left flank. They interpret the nominal exponent as suggesting that extra compute should go to model size, but say to treat the fit cautiously.
rows.check: a=0.92±0.18 with D fixed at 1e9 tokens. The authors say the optimum is not well resolved. No separate D*(C) exponent is fitted.

source_check.locator_found: Sec. II D 3, Eqs. (3)–(4); Sec. III C, Eq. (12), Figs. 6–7; Sec. IV.

rows.subject: OmniJet-α
rows.operation_detail: Compared the dataset-size power-law fit with and without its smallest-D point.
rows.measure: Sensitivity of fitted dataset-size scaling range to inclusion of the smallest-D point
rows.value: Removing this point shrinks the fitted dynamic range by a factor of 9.
rows.locator: Sec. III B; discussion accompanying Fig. 4
rows.note: The authors state that the reported power law is dominated by the smallest dataset-size point.
rows.check: This is a sensitivity to a single data point within one study, not a disagreement between published laws; it is evidence only for the fitting-choice part of V7.

Jet pT, mass, τ21, τ32, and constituent count

rows.subject: OmniJet-α
rows.operation_detail: Fit sliced Wasserstein distance against dataset size.

conditions.value: 50k generated jets compared with 50k real jets not used in training

rows.measure: Joint SWD versus unique training-token count D
rows.note: The text reports the SWD fit with its floor fixed to the measured real-versus-real value. This concerns generated-jet quality, not held-out pretraining loss or downstream-task performance.

rows.subject: OmniJet-α
rows.operation_detail: Compared model-size-dependent validation NTP loss with joint SWD.
rows.measure: Association between validation NTP loss and joint SWD
rows.value: The authors report a clear monotonic relationship; fitting SWD as a function of loss gives L0 = 7.18 and Spearman = 1.00.
rows.note: The authors describe NTP loss as a good proxy for physics performance within the tested model-size range. This is not a downstream-task evaluation.
